article_title: AI-Powered Feedback System for Writing: A Review of Automated Writing Evaluation (AWE) Tools
citation: Gres, E., Riyanti, D., & Yuliana, Y. G. S. (2026). AI-POWERED FEEDBACK SYSTEM FOR WRITING: A REVIEW OF AUTOMATED WRITING EVALUATION (AWE) TOOLS. Wiralodra English Journal, 10(2), 1–13. https://doi.org/10.31943/wej.v10i2.572
title: Automated Writing Evaluation (AWE) tools: Grammarly, Quillbot and DeepL Write
description: Automated Writing Evaluation (AWE) tools are AI-powered feedback systems for writing that provide immediate and customized feedback on learners' texts. The review examines tools "such as Grammarly, Quillbot and DeepL Write" and finds they contribute to writing precision, fluency and grammatical proficiency, and can enhance organization and overall writing quality while encouraging self-directed learning. They are the central artifact category of the reviewed literature.
requirements: Immediate and customized feedback capability to function as a writing feedback system
constraints: accuracy concerns in evaluating complex writing aspects
target_learners: L2/EFL writing learners in the reviewed 2019–2024 studies
examples: The review analyzed results from 50 empirical studies published from 2019 to 2024 covering these AWE tools
key_sources: Gres, E., Riyanti, D., & Yuliana, Y. G. S. (2026). AI-POWERED FEEDBACK SYSTEM FOR WRITING: A REVIEW OF AUTOMATED WRITING EVALUATION (AWE) TOOLS. Wiralodra English Journal, 10(2), 1–13. https://doi.org/10.31943/wej.v10i2.572

article_title: Awareness of Technological Isomorphism: Integrating AI into Elementary Mathematics Teaching on Data and Prediction
citation: Li Li, Yu Cao. (2025). Awareness of Technological Isomorphism: Integrating AI into Elementary Mathematics Teaching on Data and Prediction, A Case Study of the Compound Line Graph.
title: Awareness of Technological Isomorphism: a three-level metacognitive construct explaining cognitive transfer from mathematics to AI understanding
description: The article proposes Awareness of Technological Isomorphism, "defined as a student's metacognitive realization that their own mathematical cognitive operations (e.g., observing trends, inducing patterns, and making predictions) share an underlying logical structure with AI technical operations". It comprises three progressive levels — existence, recognition, and internalization of isomorphism — and is anchored in Ausubel's transfer theory and Flavell's metacognitive theory. The article distinguishes it from computational thinking: students need not "think like a computer scientist" but discover their reasoning is already mirrored by machine processes, which the authors argue is more developmentally accessible in elementary school.
requirements: Instructional guidance must reveal that AI performs a task with the same underlying logic students have just used, so recognition can occur
constraints: The article notes the construct was conceptualized and operationalized for the elementary 'Data and Prediction' continuum, with Stage 3 (internalization) left open for further operational development
target_learning_goals: trend estimation and data reasoning in mathematics
examples: The Grade 5 compound line graph lesson operationalized the construct through mathematical inquiry, AI prediction comparison, and reflection on prediction failures
key_sources: Li Li, Yu Cao. (2025). Awareness of Technological Isomorphism: Integrating AI into Elementary Mathematics Teaching on Data and Prediction, A Case Study of the Compound Line Graph. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09598

article_title: The core features of CSCL: Social situation, collaborative knowledge processes and their design
citation: Cress, U., Stahl, G., Ludvigsen, S., & Law, N. (2015). The core features of CSCL: Social situation, collaborative knowledge processes and their design. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 10, 109-116. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9214-2
title: Awareness tools as CSCL social enhancements that make otherwise invisible cues visible
description: In contrast to the view that computer mediation filters out social context cues, the editors describe mediational tools as offering "social enhancements to the interaction". Awareness tools "may present information about the social situation or about the group members, which would not be available in normal, non-mediated communication", including peers' knowledge, activities, expertise, status or relations, sometimes aggregated to make conclusions salient, such as activity levels or recommended learning partners.
requirements: The CSCL tool must communicate social cues about the members and the group for awareness information to be conveyed
examples: An awareness tool can provide information about peers' activity levels or recommend suitable learning partners
key_sources: Cress, U., Stahl, G., Ludvigsen, S., & Law, N. (2015). The core features of CSCL: Social situation, collaborative knowledge processes and their design. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 10, 109-116. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9214-2

article_title: Designing Academic Writing Analytics for Civil Law Student Self-Assessment
citation: Knight, S., Buckingham Shum, S., Ryan, P., Sándor, Á., & Wang, X. (2016). Designing Academic Writing Analytics for Civil Law Student Self-Assessment. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0121-0
title: AWA: a web application providing rhetorical-move highlighting as formative feedback on draft legal writing
description: AWA is a web application developed at UTS that accepts pasted plain text, invokes NLP services on the Open Xerox server, and renders output in multiple forms including highlighting of rhetorically salient sentences, move-frequency statistics, a wordcloud, and key concepts, places and people. It adopts "the metaphor of receiving feedback from a colleague who has used different coloured highlighters". Version 1 was implemented in PHP with version 2 under development in Ruby-on-Rails.
requirements: Users authenticate with university credentials and paste plain text for analysis
constraints: The system is presently available only for internal use
Designed as a prototype; students are told to be critical of its output
examples: Piloted in a UTS Civil Law degree course with 40 student volunteers submitting essays after official submission to avoid unfair advantage
key_sources: Knight, S., Buckingham Shum, S., Ryan, P., Sándor, Á., & Wang, X. (2016). Designing Academic Writing Analytics for Civil Law Student Self-Assessment. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0121-0

article_title: The impact of high-immersion virtual reality on anatomy learning, enjoyment, presence, and cognitive load
citation: Kaplan-Rakowski, R., Norton, S., & Wojdynski, T. (2026). The impact of high-immersion virtual reality on anatomy learning, enjoyment, presence, and cognitive load. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10676-1
title: Awake Heart VR anatomy tutorial
description: Awake Heart is a free educational VR application used as the instructional treatment in the study, covering names of heart components, heart functions, and potential medical conditions such as tachycardia and heart murmurs. In it, "study participants explored a highly detailed, anatomically accurate 3D model of the human heart. The treatment combined guided narration with interactive elements that required participants to identify anatomical structures." The video group watched a screencast of the identical tutorial on a standard class projector, with no pausing or rewinding.
requirements: A VR headset (Oculus Quest 2 in the study) for the immersive condition; approximately 16 minutes of session time
constraints: The article notes the intervention was a single 16-minute session, limiting inferences about sustained or cumulative learning outcomes
target_learners: college students without prior medical training
target_learning_goals: heart anatomy: component names, heart functions, and related medical conditions
examples: VR participants moved a virtual hand to study the holographic heart from all directions and clicked labels to receive lectures on heart components
key_sources: Kaplan-Rakowski, R., Norton, S., & Wojdynski, T. (2026). The impact of high-immersion virtual reality on anatomy learning, enjoyment, presence, and cognitive load. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10676-1

article_title: Multimedia-based cybersecurity and privacy professional development on educational technology for K-12 personnel
citation: Florence Martin, Min Zhuang, Erik Byker, WeiChao Wang, Julie Bacak, Lynn Ahlgrim-Delzell. (2025). Multimedia-based cybersecurity and privacy professional development on educational technology for K-12 personnel. Education Tech Research Dev (2026) 74:849–873. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10575-x
title: Awareness-Ask-Action (AAA) cybersecurity framework for K-12 educational technology
description: The AAA framework is a three-level adaptation of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's five-aspect framework (identify, protect, detect, respond, recover), tailored for an Edtech cybersecurity and privacy PD. The "Awareness" level "focuses on increasing awareness by K-12 school personnel on educational technologies used in various school districts, the data collected by these technologies, vulnerabilities associated with them, and the types of cyber-attacks". The "Ask" level helps personnel critically recognize which questions to ask software companies and understand functionality-versus-security tradeoffs. The "Action" level supports personnel as they detect, respond to, and recover from attacks. The PD's four modules were mapped onto this framework.
requirements: Content modules mapped to the framework's three levels, with topics identified by cybersecurity experts and aligned to ISTE standard 1d for Educational Leaders
constraints: Adapted specifically for Edtech cybersecurity and privacy PD for K-12 school personnel rather than for general cybersecurity training
target_learning_goals: recognize edtech data types, vulnerabilities, and common cyber attacks
ask security and privacy questions of software vendors
detect, respond to, and recover from cyber attacks on educational technology
examples: The PD's first two modules covered educational technology and data types and frequent cyber attacks (Awareness); the third covered communicating with software providers (Ask); the fourth covered steps to take proper action (Action)
key_sources: Florence Martin, Min Zhuang, Erik Byker, WeiChao Wang, Julie Bacak, Lynn Ahlgrim-Delzell. (2025). Multimedia-based cybersecurity and privacy professional development on educational technology for K-12 personnel. Education Tech Research Dev (2026) 74:849–873. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10575-x

article_title: Successful Learning of Academic Word List via MALL: Mobile Assisted Language Learning
citation: Minoo Alemi, Mohammad Reza Anani Sarab & Zahra Lari. (2012). Successful Learning of Academic Word List via MALL: Mobile Assisted Language Learning. International Education Studies, 5(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v5n6p99
title: 40-item multiple-choice Academic Word List vocabulary test (Cronbach's alpha = .89)
description: The study's measurement instrument was a researcher-built vocabulary test drawn from Coxhead's (2000) Academic Word List. A list of 100 words (10 from each of the 10 sublists) was given to students, and 40 items that students had difficulty with were turned into multiple-choice items. The article reports that "the reliability of the test calculated using Cronbach Alpha which was .89." The item order was changed for the delayed post-test to prevent a practice effect.
requirements: Piloting with similar students to establish reliability before use
constraints: Items were selected only from words students had difficulty defining, drawn from the AWL sublists
target_learning_goals: academic word knowledge (meaning, collocation, word families)
examples: The same test served as immediate post-test, with reordered questions as the delayed post-test four weeks later
key_sources: Minoo Alemi, Mohammad Reza Anani Sarab & Zahra Lari. (2012). Successful Learning of Academic Word List via MALL: Mobile Assisted Language Learning. International Education Studies, 5(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v5n6p99

article_title: Factors influencing awareness of healthcare providers on maternal sepsis: a mixed-methods approach.
citation: Brizuela V, Bonet M, Souza JP, Tunçalp Ö, Viswanath K, Langer A. (2019). Factors influencing awareness of healthcare providers on maternal sepsis: a mixed-methods approach. BMC Public Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-019-6920-0
title: Awareness as a three-component construct: knowledge, perception of enabling environments, and perception of severity of a condition
description: The article defines awareness, drawing on behavioural sciences and health communication theories, as "a combination of concepts associated with knowledge, perception of enabling environments, and perception of severity of a condition that interrelate to sensitize people towards this problem". It operationalises the three components in a 32-question survey (Table 2) and uses them to structure both the interview framework and the campaign design. The construct underpins the argument that raising awareness requires more than knowledge gains.
requirements: Measurement must cover all three components — knowledge items, enabling-environment perception items, and severity-perception items — as the survey does
constraints: The authors note awareness is oftentimes not consistently or well defined in the wider literature, and that increased awareness was not always linked with increased or correct knowledge
target_learners: Healthcare providers in participating facilities (physicians, residents, midwives, nurses)
target_learning_goals: Awareness of maternal sepsis identification and management
examples: The 32-question baseline survey mapped variables to the three components: knowledge (Q10, Q11, Q2b/Q2a), enabling environment (Q4–Q6), and severity (Q1, Q14, Q16, Q17).
key_sources: Brizuela V, Bonet M, Souza JP, Tunçalp Ö, Viswanath K, Langer A. (2019). Factors influencing awareness of healthcare providers on maternal sepsis: a mixed-methods approach. BMC Public Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-019-6920-0
